description: VFS + page cache decomposed. How Linux maps file operations through VFS to specific filesystems, with the page cache as the unifying memory layer. dentries, inode operations, file operations, page cache reads + writes, writeback, direct I/O bypass, fadvise + madvise hints.

sub_mechanisms.name: VFS_operations_struct
sub_mechanisms.definition: Function-pointer tables: super_operations, inode_operations, file_operations, dentry_operations. Each filesystem fills these in.
sub_mechanisms.why: Polymorphism in C. ext4_file_operations.read = ext4_read; nfs_file_operations.read = nfs_read. Generic VFS code calls through these pointers. The OO pattern of UNIX.

sub_mechanisms.name: dcache_dentry_cache
sub_mechanisms.definition: Kernel cache of dentries (path component → inode mappings). LRU-ish; populated on first lookup, evicted under pressure.
sub_mechanisms.why: Path resolution is hot path. Cached lookups are O(1); cold lookups walk filesystem. After warmup, virtually all paths hit dcache. Critical for FS performance.

sub_mechanisms.name: inode_cache
sub_mechanisms.definition: Cache of in-memory inode structures. Held while open files reference them or until LRU-evicted.
sub_mechanisms.why: Avoid re-reading inode from disk on every open. Combined with dcache, hot files are pure-memory operations after initial load.

sub_mechanisms.name: page_cache_per_inode
sub_mechanisms.definition: Each inode has a per-inode page cache (radix tree of pages). File data lives here when read.
sub_mechanisms.why: File-as-pages model. Read populates pages; write dirties them. Multiple processes mmap'ing same file share the same pages. Foundation of mmap + ordinary read/write.

sub_mechanisms.name: read_path_through_cache
sub_mechanisms.definition: read() looks up offset in page cache. Hit: copy to user. Miss: kernel reads from disk into cache, then copies to user.
sub_mechanisms.why: First read pays disk latency; subsequent reads of same data are at memory speed. Why repeated grep through same files is fast.

sub_mechanisms.name: write_path_dirty_pages
sub_mechanisms.definition: write() copies user data into page cache pages; marks them dirty. Returns immediately. Kernel flushes later.
sub_mechanisms.why: Writes are async by default — fast return. fsync forces flush. Dirty pages count + ratio influences kernel's writeback timing (vm.dirty_ratio).

sub_mechanisms.name: writeback_kernel_threads
sub_mechanisms.definition: Per-block-device flusher threads write dirty pages to disk. Triggered by dirty page age or ratio.
sub_mechanisms.why: Background batch writes amortise disk I/O cost. Writeback latency tunable (dirty_writeback_centisecs). If too lazy: data loss on crash; too aggressive: small writes dominate.

sub_mechanisms.name: fsync_durability
sub_mechanisms.definition: fsync(fd) blocks until file's dirty data + metadata are on stable storage. fdatasync skips non-essential metadata.
sub_mechanisms.why: Durability requirement for databases (after fsync, data survives crash). Cost: actual disk write latency. Misuse (sprinkling fsync) destroys throughput; databases group writes to batch fsyncs.

sub_mechanisms.name: O_DIRECT_bypass
sub_mechanisms.definition: open(O_DIRECT) skips page cache: reads/writes go directly between user buffer and disk.
sub_mechanisms.why: Databases that manage their own cache (Oracle, Postgres with direct_io option). Avoids double-buffering. Cost: app must align buffers + sizes to block size; no readahead benefit.

sub_mechanisms.name: fadvise_hints
sub_mechanisms.definition: posix_fadvise tells kernel access pattern: SEQUENTIAL (aggressive readahead), RANDOM (no readahead), DONTNEED (drop from cache).
sub_mechanisms.why: Apps know their access pattern; kernel doesn't. Hints improve cache behaviour. Rsync uses DONTNEED to avoid cache pollution; database scans use SEQUENTIAL.

sub_mechanisms.name: madvise_hints
sub_mechanisms.definition: madvise on mmap'd memory: similar to fadvise but for memory mappings. HUGEPAGE, NOHUGEPAGE, DONTNEED, MADV_FREE.
sub_mechanisms.why: Per-region tuning. THP can hurt or help; madvise lets per-mmap control. MADV_FREE marks pages as 'OS can reclaim without writing back' — useful for caches.

sub_mechanisms.name: sendfile_zero_copy
sub_mechanisms.definition: sendfile(out_fd, in_fd, ...) copies file data directly from kernel's page cache to socket without user-space copy.
sub_mechanisms.why: Web server static file serving: no need to copy file to user buffer then write to socket. Two copies eliminated. nginx, Apache use this. splice() generalises to arbitrary fd-to-fd.

derivation_rules.name: VFS_decouples_application_from_filesystem_choice
then: it works on any mounted filesystem
derivation_rules.why: VFS dispatches through function pointers. ext4, NFS, procfs, tmpfs all expose the same API. Application code is filesystem-agnostic. Standard Unix design — same API across local + remote + virtual filesystems.

derivation_rules.name: page_cache_makes_warm_io_memory_speed
if: file data is in page cache
then: reads are at memory speed (~ns latency)
derivation_rules.why: Cache hit: memcpy from page cache to user buffer. Miss: disk read (~ms). Hit rate dominates I/O performance. 'free' RAM is mostly page cache — visible difference for repeated workloads.

derivation_rules.name: O_DIRECT_avoids_double_buffering_for_self_caching_apps
derivation_rules.why: Database has its own buffer pool. Kernel page cache duplicates the data. O_DIRECT skips it: data goes directly to app buffer. Trade-off: lose readahead + must align — but for databases that already manage caching, win is significant.

derivation_rules.name: sendfile_eliminates_user_space_copy
if: data goes from file to socket (server use case)
derivation_rules.why: Without sendfile: read(file, buf) + write(socket, buf) — 2 copies + 2 syscalls. With sendfile: 1 syscall, kernel transfers internally. CPU savings substantial; nginx + Apache rely on this for static file performance.

derivation_rules.name: fsync_required_for_crash_durability
derivation_rules.why: write() returns when data hits page cache, not disk. Crash before flush = data loss. fsync blocks until on disk. Databases group commits to amortise fsync cost across many transactions.
